query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Wear resistance of high-entropy-alloy (HEA) coatings is governed by the magnitude of lattice distortion (atomic size mismatch δ), which enhances dynamic strain hardening at the sliding interface and thereby reduces material removal during wear.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA coating (single-phase FCC) with moderate lattice distortion (δ ≈ 3.5%).
generation.intervention: Introduce Al to partially replace Fe and Mn, increasing δ from ~3.5% to ~6.5% while keeping overall composition high-entropy and single-phase.
generation.conditions: Pin-on-disk wear tests under 10 N normal load, 0.5 m/s sliding speed, room temperature, dry atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion magnitude (δ), quantifying local strain fields that impede dislocation motion and promote work-hardening.
generation.mechanism: Higher δ increases resistance to dislocation glide and activates in-situ strain hardening under contact stresses, raising surface hardness and reducing wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: As δ increases from ~3.5% to ~6.5%, coating hardness should increase and wear rate should decrease; the effect is expected to be monotonic and on the order of tens of percent, though exact magnitudes are uncertain.
generation.baseline: CoCrFeMnNi coating with δ ≈ 3.5%, hardness ~4 GPa, wear rate ~8 mm³/N·m (pin-on-disk).
generation.boundary: Applies for δ between ~3% and ~8% under sliding speeds ≤1 m/s and temperatures ≤200 °C; beyond this, phase changes or thermal softening may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: Moderate—microstructural factors (grain size, minor phase separation) and coating defects could confound the observed correlation between δ and wear.

falsification_experiment.design: Sputter‐deposit three HEA coatings on identical steel substrates with δ ≈3.5%, ≈5%, and ≈6.5% (via controlled Al content). Perform pin-on-disk tests at 10 N, 0.5 m/s, RT.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing δ does not produce a statistically significant hardness increase and corresponding wear-rate decrease (beyond experimental uncertainty), the hypothesis is falsified.
